item.title: Some thoughts on the beginning of infinity
item.description: Some thoughts on the beginning of infinity The Beginning of Infinity presents David Deutsch’s ambitious argument that explanations are the key to solving all problems not forbidden by the laws of physics. Unlike his previous work ‘The Fabric of Reality’, Deutsch here offers a unifying theory connecting epistemology, aesthetics, morality, justice, science, and biology. The book is widely celebrated in rationalist and tech communities as a grand philosophical synthesis that could guide humanity toward unlimited progress.
item.content:encoded:
Some thoughts on the beginning of infinity

The Beginning of Infinity presents David Deutsch’s ambitious argument that explanations are the key to solving all problems not forbidden by the laws of physics. Unlike his previous work ‘The Fabric of Reality’, Deutsch here offers a unifying theory connecting epistemology, aesthetics, morality, justice, science, and biology. The book is widely celebrated in rationalist and tech communities as a grand philosophical synthesis that could guide humanity toward unlimited progress.

The main intention of this critique is to open up a dialectic around the Beginning of Infinity and examine the difficulties around establishing one. I start by examining Deutsch’s limits while explaining complex adaptive systems, transition into how this fallacy transfers to his narrative of history, and finally present a lens - the attractor - to examine why his framework is hard to escape.

To preface our discussion, in the Beginning of Infinity Deutsch often seems to change domains abruptly - he transitions from talking about scientific domains (stars/evolutionary biology/mathematical abstractions) to complex-adaptive domains (social institutions/culture/morality) in leaps. I will link to a section (Appendix 1) with a collection of quotations from the Beginning of Infinity that are what I call the Slipping Points - the exact sentence in a chapter where he stops sound science-talk and slips into generalizations about culture and history. Although after chapter 9, this is hard to do because everything is muddled. We will deal with the last few chapters in section 2 of the critique.

Apart from this, Deutsch’s epistemological core in the Beginning of Infinity is ultimately Popperian - falsifiability, criticism, and error correction - all of which I whole-heartedly agree with. So I will not be arguing against the importance of explanatory knowledge or criticism. A critique of Deutsch is not necessarily a critique of Popper.

Section 1: Seeking better explanations (for Complex Adaptive Systems)

“Outside of physics, and generally in complex domains, the reasons behind things have had a tendency to make themselves less obvious to us…” - Nassim Taleb, Antifragile

I will never understand how someone can be a Deutsch and Taleb fan at once, without reconciling the fundamental differences between them. There is a difference between the explanation OF a complex-adaptive system and explanation WITHIN a complex adaptive system. Deutsch conflates these when discussing society, culture, and politics, applying explanatory frameworks that work for physical analysis to domains where emergence and opacity dominate.

The word ‘explanation’

Deutsch uses “explanation” uniformly across physics and politics, but explanatory success means different things in different domains.

In physics, a good explanation reveals underlying mechanisms that enable prediction and control. In complex adaptive systems, Taleb shows us that knowledge often involves understanding structural properties - fragility, asymmetric consequences, black swans - while accepting fundamental limits on prediction and control.

In this section, I argue that Taleb’s explanations are better than Deutsch’s explanations for complex-adaptive systems. Even if Taleb’s ideas are no silver bullet, for my purposes I only need them to be better explanations than Deutsch’s. I will focus on Deutsch’s discussions on politics (chapter 9 discusses policies and chapter 13 discuss governance), social institutions (chapter 15 discusses static/dynamic societies), and history.

Deutsch vs Taleb: on prediction

According to Herbert Simon, human systems - institutions, markets, societies - are near-decomposable hierarchical structures whose behavior resists the kind of unified explanations Deutsch seeks. Within such systems, Simon shows we must adopt “procedural rationality” - reasoning that adapts to constraints rather than pursuing logical optimization. This directly contradicts Deutsch’s vision of universal rationality converging on objective truths.

Taleb agrees: prediction within complex adaptive systems isn’t just difficult, it’s systematically misleading (the turkey problem). He critiques the naive rationalism of being confident in the predictive power of models and theories in systems characterized by non-linearity, opacity, and ‘rare’ black swan events.

In his view, this obsession with prediction in such systems is not only futile, but harmful - as it breeds fragility by encouraging over-optimization or harmful-intervention. Deutsch is careful to distinguish between prophecies and prediction, but he still treats prediction in complex systems as fundamentally the same enterprise as in physics - just harder. This leads him to theorize about societies and institutions like he’s in physics class.

Deutsch vs Taleb: on problem solving and intervention

This is one of their main differences. Deutsch treats all progress as a chain of problems and solutions - keep solving problems, live with the solution, and solve the newer (better) problems that emerge. But Taleb forces us to ask deeper questions: which problems should be solved and which interventions risk causing more harm than good? Which problems should remain unsolved? Taleb constantly warns about the unintended damage of naive interventions that create fragility instead of progress. Deutsch’s model treats every unsolved problem as an open invitation for intervention, but in domains like economics, governance, or ecology, this approach creates what Taleb calls ‘asymmetric consequences’.

The people (or institutions) who benefit from a solution are often different from those who bear the costs of the new problems the solution creates. Deutsch glosses over the crucial moral dimension: who lives the solution, and who lives with its consequences? In complex adaptive systems, the question isn’t whether the problems are soluble, but whether the act of solving them creates more fragility, and how the costs and benefits are distributed across time and populations. Deutsch’s optimistic rationalism has no framework for recognizing when intervention itself is the problem.

Unpacking Deutsch’s ideas on political progress and social theory

Consider how this plays out in Deutsch’s treatment of political progress. He frames political progress as fundamentally developing better explanations that can withstand rational criticism, similar to how science advances. In chapter 13, Deutsch lists “..that slavery is an abomination, or that women should be free to go out to work, or that autopsies should be legal, or that promotion in the armed forces should not depend on skin colour” in the context of “convergence in the broad consensus over time is made possible by the fact that all concerned are gradually eliminating errors in their positions and converging on objective truths”. Yet this epistemological framework is misapplied to political change. All the changes he listed required sustained political struggle, activism, legal challenges, and institutional pressure - often against opponents who understood the moral arguments perfectly well but had material interests in maintaining the status quo.

But Deutsch’s framework cannot explain that the British colonization of India and the ‘British enlightenment’ happened simultaneously. The administrators simultaneously championed individual liberty at home while justifying paternalistic control in India. This wasn’t inconsistency - they had perfectly coherent explanations for both positions. The problem is that Deutsch’s framework provides no way to distinguish between genuine moral progress and sophisticated rationalization of power structures. From a Talebian perspective, their “explanations” were locally adaptive - they served the revealed preferences of their social position while maintaining intellectual coherence. The strength of democratic institutions lies not in their capacity to generate consensus around superior explanations, but in their ability to manage persistent disagreement and adapt to changing power relations without systemic collapse.

This misunderstanding of how democratic progress actually works is part of a broader pattern in Deutsch’s social theory. His framework divides societies into static versus dynamic categories, rather than fragile versus antifragile ones. To invoke Popper here, while closed societies tend to be more stable or “static” in their social order, Popper’s distinction is more about openness to critical scrutiny and reform than mere pace of change. Open societies are inherently more complex and unstable because they allow and encourage change and dissent, which can produce anxiety but also progress. But it doesn’t matter if a society is static or dynamic - what matters is whether it is fragile or not. A dynamic society that is fragile will collapse in the face of rapid change, and a static society that is antifragile will thrive off unexpected events. Instead of allowing for any nuance, Deutsch treats societies like closed systems that are either “on” or “off” in terms of creativity and adaptability. More on this in section 2.

Deutsch vs Taleb: on individual rationality and heuristics

The problem deepens when we examine how Deutsch thinks individuals should operate within these systems. Deutsch’s theory of individual rationality reveals another point where Deutsch-Taleb compatibility breaks down. Deutsch argues that “To choose an option rationally, is to choose the associated explanation. Therefore, rational decision-making consists not of weighing evidence but of explaining it.” Surely, he is not suggesting human decision making is rational in practice (cite thinking fast and slow), so a likely defense here is that Deutsch isn’t claiming people actually are rational in politics, but rather describing how they should be.

Even granting that Deutsch proposes a normative ideal rather than describing actual behavior, his framework fundamentally misunderstands what makes decision-making effective in complex adaptive systems. In environments characterized by emergence, non-linearity, and rapid change, explanations quickly become obsolete or misleading. Deutsch sees heuristics as “parochial” - temporary scaffolds that must be transcended by universal explanations. This perspective enables him to retroactively frame entire ‘failed civilizations’ as victims of heuristic thinking - a move that misjudges heuristics as primitive rather than adaptive. Through Taleb’s lens, however, heuristics are the highest-functioning form of knowledge in complex domains as they have evolved through collective trial and error. The green lumber fallacy shows that successful navigation of complex systems often requires less explanation, not more.

Deutsch universalizes an epistemological framework that may work for scientific inquiry but fails catastrophically when applied to domains where speed, adaptability, and emergent learning trump explanatory depth. A normative theory of rationality that systematically devalues what actually works in complex environments isn’t offering an ideal worth pursuing. Deutsch wants the authority of making empirical claims about how political systems actually function (chapter 13: this is the context he’s discussing ‘choices’ in), but when those claims are challenged, he retreats to normative territory.

Deutsch vs Taleb: closing thoughts

The apparent compatibility between Deutsch and Taleb exists only at the level of Popperian fallibilism - error correction and trial-and-error learning. While Deutsch’s error correction seeks to eliminate randomness and uncertainty through better explanations, Taleb’s error correction embraces randomness as information and builds antifragile systems that benefit from stressors. The issue isn’t that Deutsch ignores complexity entirely—he acknowledges emergence and abstractions within scientific domains. The problem is that his explanatory ideals, while powerful for physical systems, become systematically misleading when applied to domains governed by different structural principles.

This is why Deutsch’s historical narrative from Athens to Renaissance Italy to modern science exemplifies what Taleb calls the “narrative fallacy” - imposing retrospective coherence on complex phenomena that resist linear explanation. Deutsch achieves his neat story by systematically ignoring alternative trajectories, failed civilizations with “good” explanations, and successful societies that thrived through apparent irrationality. We will deal with his story in the next section.

Section 2: A Physicist’s Bad History

Even if Deutsch avoids determinism, he still imposes a retrospective, linear causality onto history, flattening its complexity into a neat tale of progress, all stemming from a singular spark he calls “the Enlightenment.”

The word ‘Enlightenment’

Firstly, his definition of the Enlightenment is itself easy to vary. Consider the following disclaimers from his book: “In my terminology, the continental Enlightenment understood that problems are soluble but not that they are inevitable, while the British Enlightenment understood both equally.” “Note that this is a classification of ideas, not of nations or even individual thinkers.” “In this book, when I refer to ‘the’ Enlightenment I mean the ‘British’ one.” This maneuver allows Deutsch to retroactively assign “Enlightenment values” to any figure or moment he approves of - whether it’s Babbage and Lovelace, Renaissance Italy, or ancient Athens - regardless of their historical context. By continually redefining the Enlightenment to suit his thesis, he gives the impression that all human progress can be traced back to a single intellectual lineage. He can just call all the exceptions ‘mini-enlightenments’ later.

Deutsch’s ideas about hunter-gatherer societies

In chapter 15, he dismisses hunter-gatherer societies as inherently “static societies,” arguing that “primitive societies (including tribes of hunter-gatherers) must all have been static societies, because if ever one ceased to be static it would soon cease to be primitive, or else destroy itself by losing its distinctive knowledge.” His own theory depends on what he calls “a tradition of criticism” as the key to sustained progress. If we were to consider recent scholarship, according to David Graeber and David Wengrow in The Dawn of Everything, the ideas about liberty, personal freedom, and critique of hierarchies that Deutsch celebrates didn’t originate in Renaissance Italy’s “smouldering” spark, but from “European contact with indigenous North American cultures that had long-standing traditions of debate.”

These societies had developed sophisticated political sensibilities through exactly the kind of critical discourse Deutsch claims was missing from pre-Enlightenment civilization: “not only did the North Americans manage almost entirely to sidestep the evolutionary trap that we assume must always lead, eventually, from agriculture to the rise of some all-powerful state or empire; but in doing so they developed political sensibilities that were ultimately to have a deep influence on Enlightenment thinkers and, through them, are still with us today.” The very spark Deutsch traces to Florence may have indigenous origins - from societies he categorically dismisses as “static.” Even if the wengrow/graeber scholarship is not settled, and even if Deutsch can easily co-opt the Wendats into his Enlightenment tradition - I am merely pointing out how easy it is to vary his historical landscape. More on this in section 3.

Deutsch on Athens and its contemporaries

Another example is in Chapter 9, when Deutsch contrasts Athens with Sparta to highlight the virtues of early democracy. Before analyzing Pericles’ praise of Athens, he adds a qualifier: “in assessing the optimism of a civilization, what that civilization aspired to be must be even more important than what it had yet succeeded in becoming.” This conveniently lets him ignore the social realities of Athens in 570-480 BCE, and focus on Pericles’ rhetoric, which is necessary because Athens was no cradle of freedom: it practiced chattel slavery, enforced veiling for women, and forbade them from appearing in public. Deutsch may counter that Athens would have eventually corrected these flaws thanks to its tradition of criticism. But why compare Athens and Sparta at all? Why not Athens and the Achaemenid Empire? While Athens advanced limited political democracy (for 10% of the population), Cyrus pioneered imperial tolerance and human rights, as reflected in the Cyrus Cylinder. Because Persia was a monarchy, Deutsch excludes it from his schema of progress, ignoring that people under Cyrus may have enjoyed more practical freedoms than Athenian citizens.

Deutsch and the smouldering spark in Renaissance Italy

Similarly, while discussing Renaissance Italy’s “mini-enlightenment,” Deutsch notes how “they sent agents all over the known world to obtain copies of ancient books.” He conveniently omits that these copies were preserved and expanded by Byzantine and Islamic scholars during the Islamic Golden Age. Scholars in Baghdad, Córdoba, and Cairo didn’t just safeguard classical knowledge—they expanded it in mathematics, medicine, astronomy, and philosophy, often motivated by religious imperatives. But that doesn’t fit Deutsch’s narrative, where progress begins only when religion is cast off and Western rationalism takes over. His framework depends on a Church-vs-science dynamic, which simply didn’t exist in cultures without a church-state divide. In those contexts, knowledge and faith weren’t in conflict.

Deutsch’s thoughts on historical research and rigor

This reveals how Deutsch’s historical narrative is designed to be irrefutable. Present him with Islamic scholars who developed rigorous explanatory frameworks in mathematics, optics, and experimental method, and he’ll respond that they lacked the right political institutions. Show him Indigenous societies that created sustainable institutions for criticism and debate, and he’ll point out they were eventually snuffed - destroyed by colonizers. Demonstrate that the Achaemenids created sophisticated explanatory approaches to governance and tolerance, and he’ll argue that Athens would have gotten there eventually through its tradition of criticism. Each historical counterexample can be dismissed on different grounds, while any supportive evidence proves his thesis. This isn’t just methodologically problematic - it renders his entire account of human progress immune to historical refutation.

Deutsch also systematically avoids specificity when condemning past civilizations. From chapter 9: “As we look back on failed civilizations of the past, we can see that they were so poor, their technology was so feeble, and their explanations of the world so fragmentary and full of misconceptions that their caution about innovation and progress was as perverse as expecting a blindfold to be useful when navigating dangerous waters.” This sweeping condemnation names no specific societies, time periods, or evidence. The vagueness is deliberate - it renders his theory hard-to-vary (in the wrong way). Any civilization that contradicts his narrative (like the Achaemenid Empire’s tolerance or Islamic Baghdad’s scientific achievements) can be retroactively classified as a “mini-enlightenment that was snuffed out tragically,” while any that fits his story becomes proof of his thesis.

Furthermore, in chapter 15 Deutsch claims that “we can deduce without historical research that every society on Earth before the current Western civilization has either been static or has been destroyed within a few generations.” This rests on his narrow definition of progress as advances in physical explanations and technology. A civilization that made significant strides in urban planning, governance, or agriculture would still be labeled “static” because these fields develop through tinkering and trial-and-error rather than explanatory frameworks.

Section 2 closing thoughts

These contradictions reveal a deeper methodological problem: Deutsch treats historical examples as illustrative rather than archival, selecting evidence that supports his thesis while avoiding the constraints of historical rigor. There is a fundamental confusion about what kind of argument Deutsch is making. Is he offering an empirical theory about historical patterns, or a normative framework for thinking about progress? He wants the authority of the first while enjoying the flexibility of the second. When confronted with counterexamples like sophisticated Indigenous political theory or the Achaemenid Empire’s tolerance, he can either retrofit them as “mini-enlightenments” or dismiss them as irrelevant to his schema. But you cannot simultaneously use history to ground a normative epistemology and evade the standards of historical accuracy. To explore the deeper pattern in these maneuvers, I propose the lens of an ideological attractor state, to which all evidence must eventually conform.

Section 3: The Enlightenment Attractor State

In complex systems theory, an attractor state is a configuration toward which a system naturally evolves and around which it tends to remain stable. Deutsch’s framework functions as a conceptual attractor: all cultural progress, intellectual achievement, and moral advancement gets pulled toward and reinterpreted through his specific definition of “Enlightenment values.” This creates a kind of ideological topology where every peak of human achievement must be mapped as either a precursor to, manifestation of, or deviation from his Western rationalist ideal.

This attractor effect operates through several mechanisms. First, definitional elasticity: Deutsch’s conception of “the Enlightenment” can expand to encompass any achievement he wants to claim (Renaissance Italy, ancient Athens, even individual thinkers like Babbage and Lovelace) while excluding any that don’t fit his narrative. Second, retrospective convergence: all genuine progress gets reinterpreted as moving toward his epistemic ideal, while alternative paths are dismissed as dead ends or “mini-enlightenments” that were “tragically snuffed out.” Third, normative universalization: what begins as a descriptive account of one particular cultural tradition becomes a prescriptive template for all human societies.

The three mechanisms above transform what should be a “hard-to-vary” explanation into something much more problematic: a “hard-to-escape” conceptual trap. His framework can only interpret diversity as either primitive (pre-Enlightenment) or aberrant (failed enlightenment). Deutsch constructs a story running from Athens through Renaissance Italy to modern science, achieving coherence by systematically ignoring alternative trajectories and retroactively redefining concepts.

Thus, Deutsch’s attractor model contributes to the lack of dialectic around The Beginning of Infinity. It creates a barrier of entry for alternate explanations or critiques of the work, since they would first need to avoid slipping into the attractor. Ironically, a framework that claims to champion open-ended progress actually creates intellectual conditions that make genuine criticism nearly impossible. The attractor doesn’t just distort our understanding of the past - it constrains our thinking about alternatives in the present. When all genuine progress must be filtered through Enlightenment categories, we lose the capacity to recognize or develop other forms of knowledge, other ways of organizing society, other paths to human flourishing.

Conclusion

Deutsch’s book gets its name from an Asimov book called The End of Eternity, which is about the problems arising from the editing of history with the primary goal of maximizing the safety of humanity. But in my view, it is the manipulation of history itself (regardless of the purpose) that collapses the future into one. The future opens up infinite possibilities only when you stop manipulating history (destroy the kettles).

The path forward requires recognizing that human creativity and problem-solving capacity are far more diverse and unpredictable than any single framework can contain. We need explanatory frameworks that can account for emergence, non-linearity, and genuine cultural diversity without collapsing into mechanistic reductionism.

Deutsch’s own epistemological principles, properly applied, point toward this conclusion. If we take seriously the idea that knowledge grows through conjecture and refutation, then we must preserve the conditions that allow continued conjecture. The Enlightenment attractor state threatens to close off entire regions of possibility space before they can be explored. The future remains infinite not because we’ve found the right universal framework, but because we’ve resisted the temptation to collapse solution space into a single attractor state.

It escapes me why Deutsch’s audience spends time defending Deutsch, when the true measure of a fan would be to critique him as heavily as possible, thus advancing the tradition of criticism. If so, this critique represents not a rejection of that tradition but its faithful application. The dialectic remains open and the future remains infinite.

Appendix 1: slipping points

Chapter 1 - “Much the same was true in every other field of knowledge”. And “The quest for good explanations is, I believe, the basic regulating principle not only science, but of the Enlightenment generally”

Chapter 3 - “including, not least, moral knowledge: knowledge about what to want, what to strive for.”

Chapter 4 - “ideas can be replicators too” and “explanatory theories evolve through a more complicated mechanism”

Chapter 5 - “Thus emergence is another beginning of infinity: all knowledge-creation depends on, and physically consists of, emergent phenomena.” “The same is true of creative thought in general” “and the enlightenment has made progress by bringing those other methods to bear in non-scientific fields too” and here he equates moral philosophy with physics explanations - “Both are liable to lead to morally wrong choices, just as embracing unreason or never attempting to explain the physical world leads to factually false theories (and not just ignorance).” - the word ‘leads to’ itself is a problem….. “It must be that morally right values are connected in this way with true factual theories, and morally wrong values with false theories.”

Chapter 6 - Leap at: “But that was reversed with the Enlightenment, whose quintessential idea is, as I have said, that progress is both desirable and attainable.”

Chapter 8 - “The best explanation of anything eventually involves universality, and therefore infinity.” This sounds more like a grand narrative.

Chapter 9: “And the only moral values that permit sustained progress are the objective values that the Enlightenment has begun to discover”

Chapter 13: “Arrow’s theorem applies not only to collective decision-making but also to individuals, as follows.”

item.title: Formal systems as simulators
item.description: Thinking of formal systems as simulators A formal system is a set of symbols and rules that we use to derive theorems. For example, the imaginary number system is a well-known formal system, with one of its most prominent symbols being ‘i’. Another well-known example is the symbol F commonly used to represent force in Newtonian mechanics. We often rely on the abstractions formal systems offer as frameworks for reasoning. Any formal system consists of a rule-book with symbols, axioms, and theorems derived from the axioms.
item.content:encoded:
Thinking of formal systems as simulators

A formal system is a set of symbols and rules that we use to derive theorems. For example, the imaginary number system is a well-known formal system, with one of its most prominent symbols being ‘i’. Another well-known example is the symbol F commonly used to represent force in Newtonian mechanics.

We often rely on the abstractions formal systems offer as frameworks for reasoning. Any formal system consists of a rule-book with symbols, axioms, and theorems derived from the axioms. Rather than treating these systems like static-rule books for abstraction, I propose that it is useful to take a step back and think of a formal system as a simulator, a tool we use to simulate environments, in order to conceptualize what it means for us to need to shift from one formal system to another.

Let us consider a situation where we want to find the force exerted on a cement block by a trolley. One way is to use CAD software that can simulate Newtonian mechanics to compute the resultant force. Another way would be to take the help of an abstraction, like a free body diagram (FBD) with arrows on it. In this case I’m simulating a real-world concept—say, an object being pushed. The FBD, with my interpretation of its arrows and numbers, helps determine the resultant force. If a formal system is a symbol manipulator that helps represent and model a complex concept, then it can act like a simulator for some concept you have in mind. A characteristic of both these simulators is that they help externalize concepts as a concrete set of symbols and rules – a block of wood being pushed versus a FBD of the block or a computer-simulated model.

This implies that we cannot blame a formal system for being inexpressive when it was set up to simulate something else. If I have a new concept I want to express, I need to find a formal system that has the ability to represent the ideas or phenomena I want it to. I will need to survey all available formal systems, assign meanings to the symbols and axioms, and see if the implications of the derived theorems really do express my concept. But since this sounds exhausting, we tend to create a formal system from scratch with the concept we want to express at the back of our minds.

If I built a simulator to use certain symbols that meet some criteria (axioms), the only way for the simulation to fail to express a concept is if the criteria themselves are incapable of expressing it. Similarly, the formal system was created to express my concept, but that is only my expectation. A formal system doesn’t come with meanings pre-installed. Its symbols and rules are neutral until interpreted. And its expressiveness is constrained by its interpretation. So when it no longer can express a concept, it means our expectations have shifted.

This is what it means when we say Newtonian mechanics ‘breaks’: it no longer simulates, with its symbols and theorems, the world we want to express. The expressiveness is not a formal system’s inherent property, and instead depends on how it was interpreted. Thus, the shift to a new formal system, for example quantum mechanics with its bra-ket notations, can be seen as outgrowing an older system because our expectations have evolved. Like any simulator, a formal system can only express what it was initially expected to, until it no longer can.

item.title: The academic who sold his ferrari
item.description: The academic who sold his ferrari It is commonly understood that an individual’s relationship with money has a significant impact on their approach to financial matters. A complex or difficult relationship with money may arise from experiences such as witnessing poverty, experiencing arguments over money during childhood, or being interested in science. The consequences of these early scars can manifest in adulthood as gambling, overspending, or entering academia. The psychology behind an academic’s relationship with money needs to be studied carefully but not academically.
item.content:encoded:
The academic who sold his ferrari

It is commonly understood that an individual’s relationship with money has a significant impact on their approach to financial matters. A complex or difficult relationship with money may arise from experiences such as witnessing poverty, experiencing arguments over money during childhood, or being interested in science. The consequences of these early scars can manifest in adulthood as gambling, overspending, or entering academia.

The psychology behind an academic’s relationship with money needs to be studied carefully but not academically. Many assume the first rule of academia is to ‘publish or perish’, but they are mistaken. The real first rule of academia is to disregard money entirely, even when fully funded. Any research student that wants to make money needs to be taught this lesson.

These days academics can signal their membership to academia in many ways. The most common signal is quoting Feynman, which is known to invoke godlike genius in the quoter. But in pre-Feynman days, what was the signal academics used? Feynman himself signalled his membership to academia by detailing how he turned down a higher paying job offer. This tradition is well-respected and has stood the test of time. Turning down high paying jobs is a mark of a distinguished academic but this must be done publicly. This must also be mentioned to any junior academic seeking employment as proof that they can “get a job anytime”.

These signals are often used to smoke out outsiders. For example, when Naval Ravikant said, “One Einstein is worth a legion of PhD drones,” it was clear that he’d never pursued a PhD himself. Anyone with a PhD knows that Einstein has a terrible h-index. The h-index is a trusted metric that measures academic impact. Another example is when Paul Graham said, “If it didn’t suck, they wouldn’t have had to make it prestigious.” There was no need for him to be so harsh on academia.

While the disregard for money in academia may have originated as a signal between academics, it may also have Freudian roots. It is well known that academics often have a great relationship with their parents (who may also be academics). The lesser known reason for this rapport is the aforementioned disregard for money. Nothing brings you closer to your parents than needing them to pay your bills. Some might argue, in a true Freudian spirit, that academics love their parents too much to split up the family or the bill.

Interestingly the most complicated money relationship is not between a PI and their own salary, but actually between the PI and their mentee’s salary. The PI must ensure the mentee is paid but not paid enough. The scientific hunger (publish or perish) must be kept alive. Other techniques that can be used to keep this hunger alive are requesting thesis updates in quick succession or suggesting that progress is too slow.

The importance of keeping scientific hunger (publish or perish) alive comes to light when writing an academic paper. In any academic publication, the author names are ordered in decreasing order of time spent working and increasing order of pay. To put it simply, we start with the first author and work our way up to the PI. This smooth team-work is disrupted when there are industry collaborators involved. Because industry collaborators don’t have scientific hunger (they’re too well-paid) they often ask annoying questions like “Why don’t we run more tests?” or “Why aren’t the results better?”. If the mentee did not have enough scientific hunger (publish or perish), the publication would be stalled to get better results with better methods. Thus, we would have no research published if the scientific hunger (publish or perish) of a junior researcher is vanquished.

A wide-spread misconception is that scientific exploration requires wealth and resources. This is entirely untrue. I was going to provide supporting arguments but my PI just asked for more thesis updates so I will leave the rest as ‘future work’.

item.title: In praise of Doofenshmirtz
item.description: The cultural significance of Heinz Doofenshmirtz Abstract Dr. Heinz Doofenshmirtz is a recurring character in Phineas and Ferb. He is a scientist whose inventions usually interfere with the main plot by the end of an episode. This paper analyzes Doofenshmirtz as a social figure in the 21st century. It reflects on his familial bonds, the socio-economic ramifications of his inventions, his political ideologies, and the intersection of science and humanity.
item.content:encoded:
The cultural significance of Heinz Doofenshmirtz

Abstract

Dr. Heinz Doofenshmirtz is a recurring character in Phineas and Ferb. He is a scientist whose inventions usually interfere with the main plot by the end of an episode.

This paper analyzes Doofenshmirtz as a social figure in the 21st century. It reflects on his familial bonds, the socio-economic ramifications of his inventions, his political ideologies, and the intersection of science and humanity.

The Childhood of a Tortured Genius

Doofenshmirtz grew up in Drusselstein, his parents are abusive, and he has a younger brother named Roger. This family dynamic is what drives him, forms his moral backbone, and gives him a unique worldview.

He recollects that his brother became his family’s favorite very early on. But Doofenshmirtz demonstrates incredible growth and poise when facing his rocky past. He calmly recites his backstory to Perry the Platypus without emotional agitation. He also is a caring father and throws a birthday party every year for his daughter Vanessa. He chooses not to perpetuate the cycle of abuse and is on good terms with his ex-wife, who divorced him over a sock puppet. The sock puppet symbolizes the widespread phenomenon of the hive-mind, lack of individuality, and the illusion of free will.

Platyplus - An Advanced Nemesis

Perry the Platypus is a secret agent at OWCA and Dr. Doofenshmirtz’s nemesis. Though Doofenshmirtz is thoroughly skilled at spotting Perry, he never assumes any platypus is Perry. His unwillingness to stereotype platypuses is indicative of his subtle yet eye-opening commentary about racial, gender, species, and economic stereotypes. He always briefs Perry on his plan and motivation, sometimes involving his backstories. He slowly builds Perry’s confidence and trust and gives Perry a chance to support his cause. Each time, Doofenshmirtz skillfully displays interpersonal skills such as giving someone a second chance and setting boundaries by cursing them as they leave.

Perry initially plays it cool and doesn’t seem to reciprocate his enemy — or nemesii — feelings. But eventually, when Perry catches Doofenshmirtz cheating with Peter The Panda, he is visibly hurt. He also helps set up Vanessa’s birthday party. Doofenshmirtz thus finds himself a nemesis who reciprocates his feelings through slow trust-building techniques like over-sharing.

The Morally Grey Evil Scientist

Doofenshmirtz’s ambition is to take over the Tri-state Area. Before becoming an Evil Scientist, he was in the Bratwurst business (Doofenshmirtz Quality Bratwurst). He showed loyalty to his German heritage but was disappointed by American social, economic, and cultural trends that put him out of business (Hot-dogs), which might have triggered him into being an Evil Scientist. He honed his skills in silence till he could create the deadly Hot-Dog-Vendor-Revenge-Inator. His unique insight into the challenges of bringing cultural roots to a foreign country must be capitalized on and heeded by any government deciding on immigration laws. To quote him, “I was headed to a Golden Land of Opportunity, a land with a pioneering spirit which welcomed misfits like me, but I ended up in America”.

Inventions, Science, and Human Progress

Doofenshmirtz’s inventions show unparalleled engineering skills and are custom-made for each situation (though he sometimes uses blueprints from the internet). His inventions break down or explode after one use to prevent misuse and patent violations. Applications for this single-use technique are a precedent for weapon regulations and a warning to world governments.

Another aspect of his engineering prowess is his ability to make a new device every episode within his monthly alimony check. It takes extreme craftsmanship and efficiency in design to achieve this. NASA vigorously studies his Space Launches and still struggles to launch space vessels at the Doof Budget Limit.

The Academic Epidemic

Doofenshmirtz has a doctorate that he bought online, a deep inquiry into the current state of academia itself. What is a real doctorate? Is paying for a Ph.D. program the same as purchasing a doctorate online? The latter option is cheaper — both in terms of money and time. His decision to purchase his doctorate can also be a direct attempt to assert dominance over his demanding guide (As referenced in the song I Must Impress My Professor). The show also sheds light on darker elements of academia in the song Evil For Extra Credit, where an unpaid intern goes to the extent of being Evil for college credits.

Politics as art - Performative and Intentional Satire

His political opinions reflect his values and morals and guide him through his life. As the founder of LOVEMUFFIN, he understands the intricate details of organizing a party and the secrets of politics. His expressions of political and cultural opinions are in clever metaphors or satire. In the song There’s a Platypus Controlling Me, Doofenshmirtz manages to ignite and open the minds of teenagers to propaganda and corporate greed without explicitly stating these topics. He also raises public awareness of reality TV scams and extortion in the interrupted television advertisement for the Telethon of Evil called Give Me Your Money. His education methods are simple and accessible — Mr. Fletcher immediately declares Give Me Your Money as clever satire.

Conclusion

In conclusion, Doofenshmirtz is a revolutionary and visionary figure who serves as a role model to any child watching him. His insights and opinions make one think rather than blindly accept and change our relationship with devices and technology. His inventions are a brilliant display of what hard work and having a nemesis can make one achieve.
